column1: Which object fits a reusable, parameterless report query that must act as a table source?
column2:
A view.
It exposes the shared query as a table-like interface for reporting.
Review source

column1: Which object can expose employee data to reports while omitting sensitive SSN columns?
column2:
A view.
Also restrict permissions so that reports cannot read the hidden data through another route.
Review source

column1: How can a view protect reporting queries from some underlying table-schema changes?
column2:
Preserve a stable set of output columns while adapting the view definition.
Consumers keep using the same interface when compatible internal changes occur.
Review source

column1: What can let a view support one modification that changes several base tables?
column2:
An INSTEAD OF trigger.
The trigger translates the requested view operation into the required base-table changes.
Review source

column1: What makes an updatable view read-only for a reporting role?
column2:
SELECT access without effective data-modification permissions.
A view is not inherently read-only just because it hides columns.
Review source

column1: Which object fits an explicitly called order workflow with several data changes in one transaction?
column2:
A stored procedure.
It can group the changes in an explicit transaction with appropriate error handling.
Review source

column1: Which object can return several named OUTPUT parameter values to its caller?
column2:
A stored procedure.
It can accept input parameters and copy output parameter values back to the caller.
Review source

column1: Which object can modify permanent data and return query result sets to an explicit caller?
column2:
A stored procedure.
Its result sets are not directly usable as a FROM or JOIN table source.
Review source

column1: Which object fits a shipping-cost calculation reused directly in a SELECT expression?
column2:
A scalar user-defined function.
It returns one value for inputs such as weight and destination.
Review source

column1: Which object returns parameterized customer orders that another query can use in a JOIN?
column2:
A table-valued function.
Unlike a view, it accepts parameters such as customer ID and date bounds.
Review source

column1: Which TVF type fits reusable parameterized logic expressible as a single SELECT query?
column2:
An inline table-valued function.
The optimizer can incorporate its SELECT into the calling query.
Review source

column1: Which TVF type supports procedural steps that fill a declared return table?
column2:
A multi-statement table-valued function.
Choose it for required procedural steps, not merely because the query has complex joins or aggregates.
Review source

column1: Which object can automatically record Salary changes when UPDATE statements modify an employee table?
column2:
A DML trigger.
The trigger must compare old and new values to identify actual Salary changes.
Review source

column1: What must be considered before using a trigger for a business integrity rule?
column2:
Whether a suitable declarative constraint can enforce the rule.
Use constraints for integrity rules when they satisfy the requirement.
Review source

column1: Why prefer a stored procedure over a trigger for a workflow that needs no automatic event response?
column2:
An explicit call makes the workflow and its effects easier to trace.
Reserve triggers for behavior that must run automatically at the database event.
Review source

column1: What happens to the original modification if its DML trigger rolls back the transaction?
column2:
The original modification is rolled back too.
The trigger and firing statement share a transaction rather than having autonomous transactions.
Review source

column1: Why can a non-inlined scalar UDF in WHERE be expensive on large tables?
column2:
Repeated calls can add per-row execution overhead.
Consider rewriting the logic when the execution plan shows this bottleneck.
Review source

column1: Which SQL Server 2019-and-later feature exposes eligible T-SQL scalar UDF logic within the calling query plan?
column2:
Scalar UDF inlining.
It needs compatibility level 150 or higher, eligible code, and inlining enabled.
Review source

column1: Which SQL Server 2017-and-later feature improves row-count estimates for eligible multi-statement TVF queries?
column2:
Interleaved execution.
At compatibility level 140 or higher, it can use actual function row counts during downstream optimization.
Review source

column1: What execution plan can be reused for a query that references a nonindexed view?
column2:
The combined plan for the query and expanded view.
The view does not have a separate query plan.
Review source

column1: Why keep view definitions focused rather than deeply nesting views?
column2:
Deep layers can complicate maintenance and query optimization.
Additional view layers do not guarantee a faster execution plan.
Review source

column1: Which function property is necessary for a UDF used in an indexed view expression?
column2:
Determinism.
Schema binding and the other indexed-view requirements still apply.
Review source

column1: Why must a DML trigger not serve as an application's query-result interface?
column2:
Trigger result sets are discouraged and can break calling applications.
SQL Server can allow them, but this capability is planned for removal.
Review source

column1: Why choose a stored procedure over a T-SQL UDF for logic that directly updates permanent tables?
column2:
User-defined functions cannot directly modify permanent database state.
A stored procedure can execute the required data modifications.
Review source
